request: Is a QALY a QALY, whoever gets it? Part 3: Fair innings and rescue

sources.title: Intergenerational equity: an exploration of the 'fair innings' argument
sources.finding: extra weight for those who would fall short of a fair innings

commands.speak: Now that we have seen the complaint that QALYs favour the young, here is an argument that they should favour them even more.
Alan Williams, one of the QALY's pioneers, made it in 1997: the fair innings argument.
Everyone, he argued, has a claim to a fair lifetime of health — a normal span in reasonable quality.
The dashed curve is such a life, lived to its natural end; the area beneath it is a fair innings.
Our 60-year-old has already had most of one; someone struck down at 30 falls far short.
Williams proposed extra weight for QALYs that go to those who would otherwise fall short of a fair innings.
On this view the young patient's QALYs count for more — the opposite of Harris's remedy.
The rule of rescue pulls another way: the urge to save an identified person in danger, whatever it costs.
One named patient in the news, against many unnamed patients who would gain more from the same money.
The QALY sum cannot see the difference: a named life and a statistical one weigh the same.
Defenders call that fairness to the unseen; critics call it blindness to something people really value.
So both arguments ask the same of the sum: add weight — for a lifetime cut short, or for a person we can see.
